World.title: Mother of Azerbaijani citizen detained in Russia claims son tortured, forced to speak against Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. The mother of Azerbaijani citizen Yadulla Ramiz oglu Rufullayev, who was detained by Russian law enforcement authorities, has said that her son was unjustly detained and subjected to severe torture and psychological pressure by Russian investigators.

Aliya Rufullayeva told Trend that her son had been working as a truck driver to support his three children. She said Russian authorities had brought what she described as fabricated charges against him under Article 276.1 of the Russian Criminal Code (espionage), which she said were not supported by any evidence.

“My son’s truck passed customs control without any problems and was cleared to return to Azerbaijan. However, Russian law enforcement authorities took advantage of the fact that he does not speak Russian and forced him to sign false documents. He has been unlawfully detained for one year and one month. During the investigation, Russian investigators put a bag over his head, taped his mouth shut and tortured him with electric shocks for hours. The Russian side is forcing him to give statements slandering the Azerbaijani state. My son has rejected these unlawful demands by Russian authorities, saying: ‘I would rather spend 20 years in prison than betray my state,’” she said.

The mother noted that Yadulla Rufullayev is the sole breadwinner of the family and that the family is facing difficult social conditions. She also claimed that the state-appointed lawyers provided by the Russian side had acted in a biased and inactive manner.

Another court hearing in the case is expected to take place on August 31.

Official appeals regarding the matter have been submitted to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Russia, the Office of the Ombudsman and other relevant state bodies.

Rufullayeva said her son had faced what she described as arbitrary treatment and discrimination by Russia because he is an Azerbaijani citizen, and appealed for state support to protect his rights and secure his release.

World.title: Washington hosts conference on international academic cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. A conference titled "Connecting Knowledge Beyond Borders: Research and International Academic Cooperation" was held at George Washington University (GW) in the U.S. capital.

The State Committee on Work with Diaspora said the event was organized by the U.S.-Azerbaijan Academic Network and focused on prospects for expanding scientific, academic and institutional cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States.

Fuad Muradov, chairman of Azerbaijan's State Committee on Work with Diaspora, attended and addressed the conference during his visit to the United States.

"Academic communities play an important role in strengthening ties between countries, expanding the exchange of knowledge and experience, and conveying objective and reliable information about states and peoples to the international community," Muradov said.

He praised cooperation between George Washington University and Azerbaijani universities, noting the importance of academic and scientific ties to the Azerbaijani diaspora's activities. According to Muradov, such partnerships can provide a foundation for joint research projects and long-term academic programs.

He also highlighted various aspects of Azerbaijan's diaspora policy under President Ilham Aliyev.

Sevinc Mammadova, assistant dean for global initiatives at GW's Graduate School of Education and Human Development and a professor, welcomed discussions on relations between Azerbaijan and the United States in academic and scientific circles and thanked the State Committee on Work with Diaspora for supporting the conference.

A panel discussion on academic cooperation was held as part of the conference, bringing together Azerbaijani and international scholars, professors and researchers working at universities across the United States.

The panel was moderated by Turan Waters, director of communications at George Washington University. Speakers included Fuad Muradov; Sevinc Mammadova; Lionel Howard, dean of GW's Graduate School of Education and Human Development and professor of education studies; Matt Winkler, founder of sports management programs at Georgetown University and American University and co-founder and executive director of the SEME Conference; Ali Mammadov, a doctoral researcher in political science at George Mason University and editor-in-chief of the Center for Security Policy Studies; and Can Korman, professor of electrical engineering and associate chair for graduate studies at GW's School of Engineering and Applied Science.

The speakers discussed expanding academic and scientific cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States, establishing long-term partnerships between universities, developing joint academic research programs, investing in human capital, and exchanging knowledge and expertise. They also considered ways to establish sustainable institutional partnerships.

The participants also exchanged views on the role of the Azerbaijani community in the United States in advancing academic diplomacy and how the knowledge, experience and professional networks of Azerbaijanis abroad could contribute to the development of scientific cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States.

The panel discussion concluded with a question-and-answer session.

Azerbaijani scholars living in various U.S. states also attended the conference.

The event was described as an important platform for identifying new areas of academic and scientific cooperation between Azerbaijan and the United States, strengthening ties between universities and expanding international academic networks.

World.title: NSW baby first in world to receive breakthrough epilepsy treatment
World.content:
A baby from the NSW Central Coast has made medical history, becoming the first person in the world to receive a precision medicine treatment for a rare and devastating form of epilepsy.

Eight-month-old Bohdi Higginson began having seizures at just three months old.

His mother Stephanie Higginson said his condition rapidly deteriorated, with 74 seizures recorded on his worst day.

"That was the worst day of my life," Ms Higginson said.

"It was like my heart just got stepped on … and there's nothing I could do."

Stephanie Higginson with her son Bohdi. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Bohdi was diagnosed with KCNT1-related catastrophic epilepsy, an often-fatal genetic disorder for which there was previously no known effective treatment.

Only 18 cases have ever been recorded in Australia.

'Constantly seizing and drowsy'

Bohdi was referred to paediatric neurologist Kavitha Kothur at the Children's Hospital at Westmead when he was four months old.

Dr Kothur said his seizures could last several minutes and were both unpredictable and frequent.

"He would be just unresponsive, stiffening, jerking, drooling," Dr Kothur said.

Dr Kothur said conventional medications were not working and Bohdi was losing developmental milestones, which was devastating for the family.

"Just seeing a child who was completely well … to a child who is constantly seizing and drowsy on the bed in the intensive care for almost a month," Dr Kothur said.

Dr Kothur says giving the treatment to Bohdi was "exciting" but "scary". (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

The paediatric neurologist said the condition carried a poor prognosis, with most children dying in infancy or suffering from severe disability.

Doctors and researchers at the hospital soon identified the genetic change driving Bohdi's epilepsy and a potential treatment that had been developed overseas.

Dr Kothur said the treatment had shown promising results in animal studies, but had never been given to a child, or patient with epilepsy.

"It was exciting but at the same time, it was also scary because we didn't know whether it would work or it would harm," Dr Kothur said.

A multidisciplinary team assessed the treatment through Sydney Children's Hospitals Network. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

A multidisciplinary team assessed the treatment through the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network's (SCHN) new innovative therapies pathway, designed to fast-track access to promising treatments.

Ms Higginson said she and her husband were terrified but felt they had little choice, making Bohdi the first recipient of the program.

"The alternative was I was going to lose my son. So, we thought, why not? Let's give it a go," she said.

A world first

Bohdi received his first dose of the treatment on April 21, and had his final seizure just three days later.

Dr Kothur said it was the best news of her whole career.

Bohdi had his final seizure three days after he received his first dose of the treatment. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

SCHN medical lead for advanced therapeutics Michelle Lorentzos said the last time she saw Bohdi, he was unable to keep his eyes open and had stopped smiling.

"To walk in and see this gorgeous, babbling, beautiful baby who's controlling his head and kissing his mum and really just doing everything a baby should be doing, is really quite magnificent," Dr Lorentzos said.

Bohdi has continued receiving the treatment and will need ongoing monitoring to determine its longer-term effects.

Dr Lorentzos says Bohdi's improvement after the treatment is "quite magnificent". (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Minister for Medical Research David Harris said the breakthrough was an endorsement of the pathway being rolled out across the state.

"Our health system is getting better at tuning itself to individual needs," Mr Harris said.

"Having these pathways in place that we can speed up that process is a win-win for everyone."

Ms Higginson said her son's world-first status was both daunting and special.

"It took me and his dad 10 years to have a baby, and for my son now to be leading the way in this medication. I always knew he was special, but he's just proven that he's even more special than I could ever [have] imagined."

Future of precision medicine

Bohdi's mother says her son's world-first status is both daunting and special. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Precision medicine involves tailoring treatment to the genetic characteristics of an individual patient.

In Bohdi's case, researchers used his genetic diagnosis to identify a treatment specifically aimed at the abnormality causing his epilepsy.

Dr Lorentzos said the innovative therapies pathway could ultimately benefit other children with conditions that are currently difficult to treat.

"If we have a pathway like this where we can streamline our process of assessing and delivering treatments for children, then that could actually change the lives of … hundreds of thousands of children within New South Wales," she said.

Ms Higginson said she hoped the treatment would eventually become available to other children who could benefit from it.

"There is hope ... miracles do happen," she said.

"Just keep advocating for your children because I'll never stop advocating for him."

World.title: 'Sad and disappointed' Sinner to miss first Grand Slam in seven years
World.content:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open, unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning his Wimbledon title.

Sinner beat Alexander Zverev last month for his second straight title at the All England Club, but then pulled out of the hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

The 25-year-old Italian wrote Friday that he will not be ready when the main draw begins on August 30.

"Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year," Sinner wrote in a post on X.

"We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. I'm obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there."

Sinner was the 2024 US Open champion and lost to Carlos Alcaraz in last year's final.

Alcaraz posted on social media on Thursday that he would be ready to play in New York after being out of action since April because of a right wrist injury.

The rivalry between the two has dominated men's tennis in recent years, and they met in the past three Grand Slam finals in 2025. Alcaraz took the most recent one with his four-set victory in New York.

That ended Sinner's title reign after he beat Taylor Fritz in straight sets in the 2024 final.

Sinner is 44-3 with six titles this year. He had a stunning collapse at the French Open, blowing a two-set lead while struggling in the heat in his second-round match against Juan Manuel Cerundolo.

He then sat out until Wimbledon, where his victory gave him five Grand Slam titles.

It will be the first time Sinner has missed a Grand Slam tournament since making his major debut at the US Open in 2019.

World.title: The world of model railways and the folk who build them
World.content:
For model railroaders like Peter Tonks, the worst thing you can say to him is "I like your toy train set".

"They're called layouts, but we understand and forgive people when they do call it that way," Mr Tonks from Georges River Model Railways says.

Model trains are a passion for thousands of Australians across the country.

But inspiring the next generation of railroaders is among the reasons for one of the largest model train exhibitions in regional Australia.

At its first event in 2024, Georges River Model Railway Group collaborated with Goulburn Mulwaree Council to host Goulburn Model Expo, an event taking place once again at the end of August.

Last year, close to 2,000 people attended.

"We're hoping to match that, if not more, because one of the aims is to promote to younger people the hobby because it's a good thing to learn many different types of skills," Mr Tonks says.

With more than fifty model railway layouts on show, Mr Tonks anticipates the Illawarra Model Railway layout, with a length of 45 metres, will be popular.

"I'm looking forward to seeing it, and I'm sure lots of people will be amazed at the sheer length of it," he says.

The Illawarra Model Railway Club meets regularly to socialise and share skills. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Michael Holden is the president of the Illawarra Model Railway Association, which has 50 members.

"Over the years, I've met a lot of very interesting people, very friendly people, very helpful people," he says.

"And we welcome all people."

A family hobby

Model railroader Dave Pallas says railway enthusiasts start by collecting everything and anything.

"We describe ourselves as magpies," he says.

Dave Pallas from Albion Park Rail has converted a room in his house to hold his model railway empire. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

"As you mature into the hobby, you get more specialised in what you want to model and what you want to run and the era you want to work in," he says.

"There are many different facets to the hobby," he says, which can include involving family members.

Bianca and Melinda Pallas grew up on the model railway circuit. (Supplied: Dave Pallas)

"I met Tracey at high school; she decided that it's a hobby I was going to stick with so she could either stay at home and be a 'widow' or join in."

Consequently, his daughters Bianca and Melinda have grown up around the circuit and still have working trains at the family home.

"When they were seven and nine, they won an award for building their own model railway," Mr Pallas says proudly.

Loading...

Although they share a train room, Tracey works in a smaller scale than her husband.

"Tracey enjoys doing the scenery aspects of the layouts, and I just love building things," Mr Pallas says.

Tracey Pallas enjoys creating scenes that lie either side of the train tracks her husband builds. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Ms Pallas says although there are very few women in the club scene, and the gentlemen encourage her, watching trains go around is not her scene.

"Some people enjoy watching trains go round and round in circles; I do not," she says.

"I got involved in actually looking at the world we are building, not just the locomotives that are on it."

Creating the scenery in a railway model animates it and gives the impression that it is a living installation. (ABC Archive)

Ms Pallas enjoys building Inglenook Sidings Shunting Puzzles, principally for the storytelling aspects of the puzzles.

"My first foray into the hobby was looking at what was either side of train tracks," she says.

"Whereas a lot of guys look at what's on the train tracks, I want to know what happens outside."

She is disappointed when layouts don't display scenery.

"A lot of exhibition layouts don't have any people on them," she says.

" If you're going to put a town in place, put some people there, put some cars there, put something there that makes the scene look alive. "

The art of the craft

Terry Flynn's train shed steps back in time to 1953. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Terry Flynn can't recall a time when he wasn't interested in model railways, dating back to a photo he recalls of himself as a child pushing a tin train given to him by his grandfather.

Accuracy in scale and era remain important aspects of the craft of model railways to Terry Flynn. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Terry Flynn's train line operates according to a schedule drawn in 1953. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

The engineering scientist says the hobby involves the broadest range of skills.

"Some people are interested in the technical side, some people are interested in the artistic," he says.

"Other people are interested in the social side and operating of model railways."

Mr Flynn's train shed includes four train stations in miniature designed circa 1953, a time he says was the pinnacle of the steam era as diesels had just been introduced.

His stations include Waterfall, Metropolitan Colliery Junction, Otford, and Scarborough.

"Accuracy is important on my models, and they're as accurate as they can be made at the scale they are," Mr Flynn says.

Some members of the Illawarra Model Railway Association gathered for their annual general meeting. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Like many club members, Mr Holden was introduced to model railways when he was a child.

"Mum and Dad bought me a Hornby train set, which I used for many years," he says.

"I'm sure if more younger people knew what this is all about, and had an opportunity to come to a club like ours, it would be a worthwhile hobby for them too."

World.title: Can the Liberals topple Victoria's government at the state election?
World.content:
The Victorian state election is less than 100 days away.

After 12 years in opposition, the Liberal and National parties could finally be in a position to topple Labor on polling day, November 28.

Still, recent opinion polls suggest One Nation will be a player.

So, where is the Coalition looking to pick up seats?

How might One Nation affect the result?

And could Labor hold its ground?

Loading...

What is the state of play in the lower house?

There are 88 seats in Victoria's lower house, meaning a party requires 45 to govern.

Labor won 56 seats at the last election. The Coalition has 29, with the Liberals holding 20 and the Nationals nine.

Three Greens MPs hold the remaining seats.

But after three terms in power, some Labor insiders fear the party could lose upwards of 20 seats in November.

To govern on its own, the Coalition would have to hold all its existing seats and win at least another 16.

This is a steep hill to climb, made even more perilous after One Nation's appearance on the scene.

A minority government, where no party reaches 45 seats, is a genuine prospect.

Ben Carroll has made crime a focus of his leadership ahead of the election. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Where is Labor in danger?

Labor faces multiple risks: Melbourne's west and north-western suburbs, the eastern suburbs, peri-urban communities, and the regions. The Greens are also chasing Labor in inner-city seats.

After three terms in power, Labor is battling a mood for change.

Melbourne's west and north-west

Labor has represented electorates in Melbourne's outer west and north-west for generations.

But first-preference votes for the party in these communities crashed at the last election, eroding Labor's buffer.

To appeal to these voters, new Premier Ben Carroll has made crime a centrepiece of his leadership since taking over last month.

Sunbury, Sydenham, Melton and Yan Yean are in danger of falling to One Nation or the Coalition.

Traditional Labor seats on Melbourne's western and north-western edge including Sunbury, Sydenham, Melton and Yan Yean are in jeopardy. (ABC News)

But even the premier's seat of Niddrie, north-west of Melbourne CBD, held with a 6.7 per cent margin, is not a sure thing.

The Coalition has Mr Carroll's electorate on a hit list of more than 30 Labor seats.

Labor believes the leadership change from Jacinta Allan to Mr Carroll has given voters a reason to reconsider, particularly in the heartland.

Melbourne's east

The Coalition must win back Melbourne's eastern suburbs if it has any chance of retaking government, Redbridge pollster and former Labor strategist Kos Samaras says.

Bayswater, Ashwood, Glen Waverley and Box Hill are in play.

Seats in Melbourne's east such as Bayswater, Ashwood, Glen Waverley, Box Hill and Pakenham will be crucial battleground seats for the Coalition. (ABC News)

Mr Samaras says there are signs the Coalition is making headway there.

Labor expects to lose Pakenham on Melbourne's suburban fringes, with Victorian One Nation leader Warren Pickering contesting this ultra-marginal seat. Crime and local infrastructure have been sore points for the government here.

Warren Pickering will lead One Nation into the Victorian state election. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

Bass and Hastings, which stretch into rural communities south-east of Melbourne, are also held by tiny margins, and Labor is not counting on holding on.

Current MPs in some of these at-risk electorates — Pakenham, Melton, Bayswater and Bass — are also retiring from parliament in November.

The regions

The Nationals are chasing former premier Jacinta Allan's seat Bendigo East after voters in the overlapping federal electorate bucked the national trend and almost unseated Labor last year.

Ms Allan confirmed she would not recontest the election after 27 years as the local MP.

Andrew Lethlean is a publican and is the Nationals' candidate for Bendigo East. (ABC Central Victoria: Shannon Schubert )

The neighbouring seat of Bendigo West could also be in play.

And Labor faces a tough, crowded contest in Ripon, in Victoria's west, which has a history of flipping.

One Nation is eyeing off regional seats such as Ripon, Murray Plains, Bendigo East, Bendigo West and Gippsland East. (ABC News)

The government's emergency services levy has been particularly potent for the regions.

One Nation could win these seats, too.

Along with the outer-suburban ring around the city, the regions are where One Nation is likely to make the most headway.

What are the risks for the Coalition?

The Coalition is optimistic it can retake government under Liberal leader Jess Wilson.

But the Liberal and National parties are under threat, too.

Their commitment this week to ditch the VNI West transmission line project through farmland hints at One Nation's threat in regional communities.

Coalition pledge could win back farmer votes West Victorian farmers, increasingly supportive of One Nation, welcome the Coalition's announcement to scrap a controversial transmission line.

The Nationals believe their incumbent MPs, at least, will hold on.

Longstanding MPs are retiring in Murray Plains and Gippsland East.

Insiders argue Nationals candidates will benefit from preferences much more strongly than One Nation, which they believe would need a primary vote above 40 per cent to beat the Coalition.

Mr Samaras agrees.

He expects One Nation will pick up lower house seats, but says its vote is softening.

One Nation's stated aim is to take government in Victoria but has so far announced only a handful of lower house candidates.

Pauline Hanson says she'll work with anyone to get rid of the Victorian Labor government. (ABC News)

Labor has sought to tie Ms Wilson to One Nation, arguing the Coalition won't be able to reach 45 seats on its own. The opposition rejects this.

Research by Labor, briefed to ministers in June, claimed One Nation could take as many as 17 regional and outer-suburban seats from the Coalition.

Labor named six Nationals-held seats as easy One Nation gains.

Outer suburban Liberal seats like Rowville and Berwick could come under pressure.

The Liberal Party also needs to prepare for the likely loss of Prahran in inner Melbourne, after winning the seat at a by-election that Labor didn't contest.

If the Greens retake the seat, the Coalition will need to gain 17 others to form a majority government.

Can Labor gain ground?

Labor knows it will go backwards this election.

Its defensive campaign means there are no Coalition seats in its sights.

But the party has been chasing a victory in Richmond, which the Greens have held since 2022.

Labor will also have to fend off the Greens in inner-metro seats like Northcote and Footscray, though.

Ellen Sandell is leader of the Victorian Greens and the state member for the seat of Melbourne. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Integrity has been a sore point for the government in the inner city.

Labor now believes it can hold on here after the announcement of a royal commission by Mr Carroll and commitment to strengthen the anti-corruption watchdog sooner.

Landing a teacher pay-deal, struck this week, was also key for these electorates.

Yet early polls, by Resolve in The Age and Redbridge in The Australian Financial Review, have actually shown a slump in primary support for Labor following the leadership change. This was within the margin of error.

One insider said voters still needed to see more from Mr Carroll.

"But they are up for listening," they said.

"And that is a big change."

World.title: Victorian premier vows to open 10 free dental clinics
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll has committed to opening 10 free public dental clinics if re-elected in November, in a soft launch of Labor's re-election pitch focused on the cost of living and health.

Anyone would be able to access the walk-in clinics. The government said they would have capacity to treat more than 100,000 patients annually at a cost of $230 million over three years.

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt told the ABC some of the clinics could be operational from July 2027. The government has not confirmed when the full 10 will be up and running.

Mr Carroll, who took over the leadership last month, is expected to lead a campaign rally in Melbourne's north-western suburbs on Saturday morning as Labor attempts to beat current polling trends and win a fourth term.

Ben Carroll and Gabrielle Williams at their first cabinet meeting as premier and deputy premier on August 4. (ABC News)

As it stands, the waitlist for public dental care — open only to eligible Victorians such as those with a healthcare card — is more than 12 months. The government said these existing services, which treat tens of thousands of Victorians a year, would continue under the proposal.

Seven in Melbourne, three in regions

Seven clinics available to everyone would open in Melbourne and three in regional Victoria, the government said. Their locations and details about the workforce required will be announced in the coming weeks.

Under the plan, patients would be able to get free check-ups and treatment such as fillings, root canals and extractions. Urgent patients would be treated first.

The state government expects some of the dental clinics would need to be built, but others could be co-located with existing services like urgent care clinics.

"I'm fighting for the tens of thousands of working people who can't afford to see a dentist," Mr Carroll said in a statement.

"This is not a one-off boost — it's structural cost-of-living support, and it's a national first."

Ben Carroll has said he wants to instil a reinvigorated sense of confidence in the Victorian economy. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

Medicare does not include dental

Medicare, a Commonwealth responsibility, does not include dental. The federal Greens have for years called for dentistry to be covered.

Victoria has previously pursued policies — occasionally outside its remit at a cost to the state despite budget constraints — in order to pressure the federal government to take responsibility.

Former premier Daniel Andrews and his NSW counterpart Dominic Perrottet in 2022 jointly promised to open priority primary care clinics with GPs as key planks of their re-election pitches.

The states heaped pressure on the Commonwealth to improve primary health care, and the Albanese government now funds some of those clinics, renamed Medicare Urgent Care Clinics.

Victorian Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said the promised dental clinics would work like those sites.

World.title: CFMEU inquiry lays bare alleged link between bikie gangs and construction sites
World.content:
Motorcycle groups trying to muscle into the Queensland construction sector have long been speculated about, but the connection was laid bare at this week's block of hearings into the CFMEU.

The connection between outlaw motorcycle gangs and the construction sector, including the CFMEU, had been established in Victoria ahead of the militant union being placed into administration in 2024.

But at the Queensland inquiry this week, it was not the CFMEU that had the alleged connections raised against them in the inquiry. It was people associated with one of the developers behind a major state government infrastructure project.

Comancheros attempted to muscle into Qld, inquiry hears The CFMEU inquiry has heard evidence that outlaw motorcycle gang the Comancheros sought to set up its own construction companies in Qld.

That project was the Centenary Bridge upgrade at Jindalee in Brisbane's west.

BMD Group and Georgiou group were the two main contractors on the project, which had been subject to ongoing disputes with the CFMEU.

The state government estimated that disruption, along with other factors, blew out the cost of the project from $298 million to $353 million.

In response to that dispute, BMD hired HOST, run by Gary Samuel, to provide security at the site.

Threats at construction site

Much of the week has focused on one specific incident on June 5 2024, when a member of the Comancheros allegedly threatened a crane operator on the construction site.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda said Mr Samuel had been on the phone and texting throughout the morning with senior management from contractor BMD, as well as Bemir Saracevic, the former national president of the Comancheros motorcycle gang.

Mr Gisonda alleged it could be inferred through phone records that Mr Samuel then picked up Mr Saracevic and associates Krstomir Bjelogrlic and Mark Ahern from Brisbane Airport, where they arrived from Melbourne, and drove them near a construction site.

CCTV footage played to the commission this week showed Mr Saracevic threatening CFMEU delegate Cody Raymond at the construction site.

Bemir 'Benji' Saracevic is former national president of the Comancheros motorcycle gang. (Supplied)

In a workplace interview about the incident, Mr Raymond said Mr Saracevic had said to him: "Do you know who the f*** I am ... Benji, from the Commos."

"He responded with 'I'll f***en burn your house down c*** and kill your kids' brother … I f***en know where you live brother," he said.

CCTV footage from before the incident captured BMD general managers Rob Pickard and Steve Thomas — who were both taking calls from Mr Samuel that morning — leaving a nearby sushi restaurant just minutes before the Comanchero members and Mr Samuel left the same restaurant.

The footage showed the duo walking several metres ahead of the group and making hand gestures.

It was put to both Mr Pickard and Mr Thomas they were signalling who Mr Raymond was to the group a few metres behind them.

They both denied that suggestion and any knowledge or involvement in the alleged threats made to Mr Raymond.

Mr Pickard also denied having conversations with Mr Samuel at the BMD head office earlier that day.

CCTV footage access issues

Queensland Police requested CCTV footage of the alleged incident in November 2024, but the inquiry heard they were told by BMD that footage from that time was unavailable.

Mr Gisonda asked Mr Thomas whether he and Mr Pickard had discussed obtaining and deleting the CCTV footage.

"I don't recall … I don't believe that's what we've done," Mr Thomas said.

The CFMEU inquiry has heard men linked to a bikie gang approached a worker at the Centenary Bridge site in 2024. (Supplied)

Gareth Davie, the corporate construction manager for Georgiou Group, told the inquiry that Mr Thomas was "a little concerned" about the CCTV footage and "wanted to lock it down".

"So we ended up reducing [access] from ... 10 or 11 people that had access to it down to down to three," he said.

But while the companies had locked down the footage, the inquiry heard project manager Quinn Murray had made a copy of the footage on the day as he felt there was something "fishy" going on.

Georgiou Group corporate construction manager Gareth Davie at the CFMEU inquiry in Brisbane. (Supplied)

Mr Davie told the inquiry he agreed it was "pertinent to gather as much contemporaneous evidence as necessary".

BMD manager caught in car with suspected bikie

The commission was played footage of police undertaking a routine traffic stop in August 2025.

Mr Thomas can be seen in that footage, alongside a man named William Samra.

Loading...

Mr Gisonda told the inquiry Mr Samra was believed to be a member of the Comancheros.

"We were just having a social catch-up," Mr Thomas told the hearing.

He said they were introduced by Mr Samra's father and had mutual friends, and he did not know Mr Samra was an alleged member of the Comancheros.

'Commercial push' from Comancheros

Mr Gisonda told the inquiry on Wednesday unnamed intelligence agencies had information the Comancheros had already installed union delegates on construction sites in Victoria.

"The Comancheros had taken measures over the preceding 12 months to establish their own companies that could operate in the construction industry in Victoria, most particularly labour hire companies," he said.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC. (Supplied)

"Victorian members of the Comancheros had travelled to Queensland in the months prior to May 2024 with the aim of achieving those two objectives in the state of Queensland as well."

He said the intelligence was not union, site or contractor specific, but rather a "general commercial push" by the Comancheros.

'Zero tolerance for violence'

CFMEU Administrator Michael Crosby release a statement on Thursday afternoon stating the incident where Mr Raymond was threatened was "extremely distressing".

"The evidence in the Inquiry over the last few days should shock the whole industry, and the Administration renews its call that the clean-up of the industry must focus on more than the previous actions of the union," he said.

Deputy premier refuses review into BMD BMD came under scrutiny in the CFMEU commission of inquiry this week, amid allegations it hired a security company linked to the Comancheros outlaw motorcycle gang in 2024.

"The new CFMEU has zero tolerance for violence.

"The Administration is tasked with removing all unlawful activity or use of violence. We expect the employers to be held to the same level of account."

Mr Crosby said there were questions remaining about what senior executives at BMD knew about the "use of Comancheros to threaten the CFMEU delegate".

"It is morally repugnant and must be condemned by all."

World.title: Guilt and isolation: Genocide survivors on adjusting to life in Australia
World.content:
The United Nations calls them "the most persecuted minority in the world", but now 10 years on from a genocide, members of the Rohingya people are rebuilding in Australia.

The Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic group, have lived in mainly Buddhist Myanmar for centuries, where they have suffered killings, forced evictions and other atrocities.

As the community in Australia continues to grow, some live in constant fear about the state of their loved ones who remain abroad.

In 2017, the Myanmar military marched into northern Rakhine — a Rohingya territory — beginning a sustained campaign of violence, forcing more than 700,000 people to flee for nearby Bangladesh.

A Myanmar police officer, pictured in 2017, at a checkpoint in Buthidaung, Rakhine State. (AP)

Saddam Hossain was one of them, escaping over the Bangladeshi border amidst the chaos.

President of the Rohingya United Youth Network and community spokesperson Robi Alam translated for Mr Hossain as he described to the ABC how Myanmar's military surrounded his village in 2017.

"They started attacking anyone, shooting everywhere," he said.

The military surrounded Mr Hossain's town in 2017 and started shooting "anyone, shooting everywhere". (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Concerned for his cows, Mr Hossain went to release them so they could escape, putting himself in the firing line in the process.

"When [I] was cutting the rope to release the cows [I] was shot on [my] right upper thigh and by the time [I] was looking to see the wound … [I] had got another two shots on [my] left thigh," the translator said.

The family escaped to a nearby village, but after three days with badly injured legs and no medical treatment, they decided to flee the region.

Mr Hossain was shot multiple times in his legs and spent four years in and out of hospital at the Cox's Bazar camp. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

"Usually ... to go to the borderline, it takes about an hour on transport," Mr Alam said. "It took them seven days, because two people had to carry him."

Finally canoeing into Bangladesh, Mr Hossain found himself at the refugee camp in the port city Cox's Bazar, which has become home to more than one million stateless Rohingyas.

After four years in and out of the camp's hospital, Mr Hossain secured a UN humanitarian visa and joined a Rohingya community in Australia, which advocates estimate is made up of about 5,000 people.

Rohingya refugees stand on their capsized boat before being rescued in the waters off West Aceh, Indonesia. (AP: Reza Saifullah)

Despite his new home, Mr Hossain said the pain hasn't gone away.

"[I feel] that … [I look] alive on the outside … [I don't] feel that on the inside at all," Mr Hossain said.

Rohingya siblings fleeing violence hold one another as they cross the Naf River along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border in Palong Khali, near Cox’s Bazar in November, 2017. (Reuters: Adnan Abidi)

Mr Hossain is thankful that he is now in a place where he can express his suffering, and grateful to his wife for taking care of him.

But after losing his father and two uncles, he is still concerned for his brother, who remains in the Bangladesh camp.

"What he wants is for the Australian community to know about the injustice against his family and community, and he wants justice," Mr Alam said.

Fears for family still in camp

Shofika Begum also came to Australia on a humanitarian visa after spending time in the Bangladesh camp, and remembers her family being killed when the military surrounded her village Arakan in 2017.

She said she was forced to watch her sister's murder.

"She had this sort of valuable hijab, and they took it off from her and just smashed her skull with that thing," Mr Alam said, translating for Ms Begum.

"And she doesn't remember anything afterwards."

Shofika Begum says she saw large portions of her family killed before escaping the genocide in 2017. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Now safe in Australia, Ms Begum shares Mr Hossain's fears for those left behind.

"She's got one more sister in the camp, two brothers [also in the camp] and two brothers in Malaysia," Mr Alam said.

" And she's just very worried for them because they're still not receiving any sort of help. "

While Ms Begum is grateful her children won't grow up in perpetual fear, the mental scars from her ordeal remain.

"[I] can't sleep at night, [I] feel that [my] mum is right next to [me]. [I] feel that [my] sister is playing next to [me]," she said.

"There's just so much in [my] head."

Saddam Hossain and Shofika Begum both escaped to the Bangladesh refugee camp before coming to Australia. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Speaking out to keep identify alive

Mr Alam was born in the Bangladesh refugee camp, and after 10 years his family came to Australia as part of the humanitarian assistance program.

He started community work when he was 14 or 15 and hears stories like Mr Hossain's and Ms Begum's "almost on a daily basis".

"Every Rohingya that we meet has stories like this and it's getting to a point where it's normalised and sometimes you just get so dehumanised that … your emotions don't react as it should after hearing such horrific stuff because of how normal it is in our community," he said.

"It just breaks you and sometimes you feel hopeless.

" But you also know that you've got to do something, and you just can't stand still. "

Robi Alam was born in the Cox's Bazar camp where he spent his first 10 years before coming to Australia. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Mr Alam said he didn't want to see the community lose its identity.

"The most fundamental thing for me is, and a lot of Rohingya people feel this, is that because of the genocide that our community has been going through over the last four or five decades, we feel that our identity is almost becoming extinct," he said.

"That's why it's a strong sense of responsibility for me to be able to do whatever I can in my capacity, because we don't want to lose who we are as a community.

" And I don't want to lose who I am as a Rohingya as well. "

The Rohingya community is hosting a Genocide Remembrance Day event later today in Kingston in Logan, organised by community organisations Rohingya United Youth Network, Australia Rohingya Council, Burmese Rohingya Association in Queensland and Rohingya Community of Queensland.

World.title: Residents gear up to keep McDonald's out of 'slow' town
World.content:
A regional town that already has 38 eating places and international accreditation as a "slow city" is gearing up to fend off one of the world's biggest fast-food chains.

The coastal town of Goolwa, south of Adelaide, is a bustling hub of small businesses that, during summer and tourism periods, are packed to the hilt with customers.

It is a place of renowned heritage at the edge of the Coorong and featured in the classic 1976 Australian film, Storm Boy.

The historic PS Oscar W is among tourist attractions at Goolwa. (891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn)

Cittaslow Goolwa, a volunteer group devoted to protecting the area's food and cultural identity, told the ABC this week that a property was under contract to buyers who wanted to build a McDonald's on the site as Goolwa's first fast-food outlet.

"All up, there are 38 eating places in Goolwa alone, without the outlying towns," said Olaf Hansen, seafood specialist and founder of cafe and restaurant Bombora On The River.

"I bet you won't find any other place in Australia that will have that many eating places, so I can't see the point of putting more in because the operators are struggling to find staff already.

"It's OK through winter but come summer, everyone is in the same boat."

He said Goolwa had a range of restaurants, including Indian, Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, German and an "iconic" fish-and-chip shop by the Murray Mouth.

"Why would you wreck the character of this town by putting fast food in it? It will probably only open the floodgates for the future," Mr Hansen said.

Some Goolwa residents do not want to see McDonald's famed arches in their town. (ABC News)

Alexandrina Council Mayor Keith Parkes said the council was aware that a property on Hutchinson Road, which leads into town from Middleton, had been up for sale and was now under contract.

"We know that there's an application for this property. It's in a commercial precinct, so the actual commercial component of the planning requirements are okay," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"It was an automotive repair facility and currently is a car wash also, so it's a change of use, and that won't come to the council for a decision."

He said it would go to the Fleurieu Regional Assessment Panel (FRAP) instead.

An accredited Cittaslow town

In March 2007, Goolwa was accredited by Cittaslow International as the first Cittaslow town in Australia, a term that means "slow city".

A delegation from Italy travelled to the regional town to present it with a certificate. Cittaslow Goolwa now has about 250 volunteer members.

A Cittaslow delegation travelled to Goolwa to present the council with a certificate in 2007. (Supplied: Cittaslow Goolwa)

Vice-president Christine Putland said the Cittaslow organisation grew out of the "slow food movement".

She said in Italy, it had been observed that slow food had resisted the loss of communities to larger corporations, supermarkets and "multinational fast-food companies".

"Their response to that was to really focus on what they could grow and produce and share locally, so that's how Cittaslow started," she said.

It also takes a broader approach to respecting and upholding a place's past and traditions, its people and meeting places, its heritage and culture.

"In Goolwa, we already have a lot of outlets. We have hamburgers already made by local businesses, for instance," Ms Putland said.

Christine Putland says a fast-food outlet is out of character with the area. (891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn)

She said it did not need to rely on a "multinational company" to create more.

"Even if the franchises might be more local or state-based, it is still not growing out of the community," Ms Putland said.

"It's not really benefiting or strengthening or capacity building in our community.

"It's not within the character of our community or our town to incorporate something like a McDonald's, or any other fast-food chain."

Public consultation expected

Cr Parkes said that once an application was made to the FRAP, it would "almost certainly go out for public consultation, over at least a two to three-week period, and that'll be advertised".

"At that stage, all members of our community, including Cittaslow and the council, will be able to submit their opinion either for, or against," he said.

Aside from a McDonald's at the top of the Fleurieu Peninsula at Aldinga, there is only one other McDonald's on the peninsula.

It is located about 17 kilometres to Goolwa's west at Victor Harbor.

Local architect Steve Grieve said a fast-food franchise would not bring anything that reflected Goolwa's historic nature.

"They just bring some American-standard international building, arches and the whole, so they don't add anything to it," he said.

"In fact, they detract from a good environment significantly."

World.title: Steven King promised his team would be selfless, ruthless, connected. But there’s one word that defines his Demons
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Steven King promised his team would be selfless, ruthless, connected. But there’s one word that defines his Demons Peter Ryan August 22, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

When Melbourne coach Steven King presented at a media briefing about the ambitions for his group in 2026, the coach’s optimism for the group’s immediate prospects was higher than most of the journalists in the room. King emphasised a pre-season based on high-speed running and vowed that the team would play a quick, modern style of football. Melbourne coach Steven King has built a strong rapport with his players in his first year at the helm. Getty He wanted the team to be selfless, ruthless and connected as they started their first year without either Christian Petracca, Clayton Oliver, and as it turned out, Steven May, on the list for the first time since 2015. The injured Jack Viney was unlikely to play much of a part in the season either.



The Demon dynasty anticipated in the afterglow of the 2021 premiership looked more like a failed state. A rebuild on the run seemed the most likely path as no one doubted the young talent at King’s disposal. View post on X The Demons’ recruiting team had not rested on the strategy Tim Lamb and Jason Taylor have employed to great effect for the past decade, with two first-round picks added to the list at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 national draft (they will have two first round picks again in 2026). But those players – Caleb Windsor and Koltyn Tholstrup (picks seven and 13, 2023), Harvey Langford and Xavier Lindsay (picks six and 11 in 2024), and Xavier Taylor and Latrelle Pickett (picks 11 and 12 in 2025) – had just 95 games experience between them when the siren sounded to kickstart round one.



And Max Gawn, Jake Lever and Ed Langdon shaped as the most likely contributors among the dozen players on the list aged above 30, with Brody Mihocek and Jack Steele recruited to keep them company over cups of tea. While King had impressed Melbourne’s coach selection panel, he remained a first-time coach, and no one was certain about how he would handle the hot seat. Now we know. King talks tough with his players. via Getty Images His coaching had an effect akin to running hot water over a tight jar lid, opening up a side of the Demons we had not seen. Under King, the blue-collar battlers have become the daring Demons, with their exhilarating upset win over ladder leaders Fremantle in round 22 making them genuine premiership contenders.



Post-match, King’s words to his players have summed up his approach perfectly. “I could throw up numbers, but they don’t really matter,” King said. Internally, the same word keeps coming up. Three people we spoke to for this article who wished to remain anonymous to speak freely, were asked what is behind their unexpected rise, they all replied, “fun”. Fun is not a word anyone has attached to Melbourne for a long time, but King – who is said to have a very dry sense of humour – brought a philosophy to celebrate players’ strengths and encourage them to bring them to life through hard work.



He can deliver hard truths when required, and knows the game exceptionally well, having done a true apprenticeship playing football at Geelong and St Kilda under Gary Ayres, Mark Thompson and Ross Lyon (he won a flag with the Cats) before coaching at the Western Bulldogs (where he was involved in the 2016 flag and 2021 grand final), the Gold Coast and then the Cats. He gives his players freedom, instilling belief by referring to their strengths, and has been a popular, respected figure at each of the clubs he served. Melbourne are genuine premiership contenders in 2026 Getty Images King also studied hard, throwing himself into a football manager’s course at the Cats while simultaneously coaching the midfield and sacrificing family time to pursue his ambition. He is off to a good start. One competition source who has watched him evolve said he has taken anxiety out of his players’ minds. Funnily enough, he has done the same to Melbourne supporters who gave him a standing ovation after the win over the Dockers.



The Demons – who built a strong foundation to their game under Simon Goodwin – have now won six of their seven matches since being seventh on the ladder at their bye. Their scores from turnover per game sits second only to Geelong in the past five matches, and they generate scores from their defensive half at a higher percentage than any other team in that time. Only Sydney has generated more scores from centre bounces in the past five games. Their football is exciting, a front-running style, akin to Vo Rogue or Pride of Jenni, which dares other teams to go with them. They are in the top four for scoring, but concede scores, too, sitting 14th for points against. All that has put them fifth on the ladder heading into the final round, having cocooned the football department from potentially destabilising events, such as the departure of the CEO and legal action against the club over what was allegedly said in a meeting called to discuss May’s absence from the group.



During the week they re-signed emerging midfielder Tom Sparrow, who had a mighty offer from Port Adelaide, having retained Kade Chandler, who has built a career through hard work to be recognised in 2026. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Melbourne dealt massive finals blow as star forward’s ban upheld A win over the Western Bulldogs – without leading goalkicker Jacob van Rooyen who is suspended – on Saturday is needed to consolidate a spot inside the top six, and could, if others stumble, hand them a top four spot. King has led the team into finals in his first season, with wins over Hawthorn, the Brisbane Lions and Fremantle on his resume. Alongside Fremantle’s Justin Longmuir and Carlton’s Josh Fraser he is destroying the myth that ruckmen can’t coach. Ever the optimist, King is not too worried about where they finish.



“I think you can win it from anywhere,” he said. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Meghan set to star in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series on return to UK
World.content:
CultureTV & radioMeghan, Duchess of Sussex Meghan set to star in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series on return to UK India McTaggart , Lily Shanagher and Victoria Ward August 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Duchess of Sussex is set to star in a Guy Ritchie Netflix series when she moves to the UK. The Telegraph understands that the Duchess is in advanced discussions to join the cast for the third series of The Gentlemen. It is unclear how many episodes she will be appearing in. The Duchess of Sussex, pictured in Australia in April 2026, is set to return to acting. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP The action series stars Theo James as a British aristocrat who inherits his family’s estate and discovers it is home to an underground cannabis empire. News of the Netflix role comes after entertainment sources told news.com.au on Thursday that the former Suits actress had been offered a part in an upcoming project based in Britain, which sources close to the Sussexes have not denied.



The Telegraph revealed on Wednesday that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were returning to the UK later this month, with their children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, already enrolled at a British school before September. Related Article Analysis

Royal family For Harry and Meghan, going home might just reopen old family wounds It is understood the offer of the role, which was only made recently, formed part of the decision-making process in the family relocating to the UK but was not the sole reason. The Duchess worked as an actress before meeting Prince Harry, and was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits. In 2017, she went on an acting hiatus and told the BBC that she viewed her career break as “a new chapter”.



She returned to acting for the first time in nearly 10 years, playing herself in the upcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, starring Lily Collins and Brie Larson. Meghan finesses a sponge cake with her make-up artist, Daniel Martin, in her Netflix series With Love, Meghan. The family intends to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence thought to be outside London later this month. The Duke and Duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals will remain unchanged. It is understood that the King was not aware of the move until last Sunday, but he is said to be pleased his younger son is coming home and is looking forward to spending more time with him and his family.



The Telegraph understands Harry – who misses the UK and wants to be closer to his wider family – hopes to regain the King’s trust by no longer discussing private family matters in public or giving television interviews. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? Prince Harry has spent years revealing details about the monarchy and his personal life. However, the couple plan not to expose their children to the public eye and British media organisations have been urged by the regulator not to disclose the location of the new family home or the children’s school. The Duke, whose own private security team claimed he was the focus of six terrorist plots, has long fought to be guaranteed police protection, but this has so far been rejected by the courts and the Home Office committee responsible for such decisions. But the family’s return is set to prompt a review of taxpayer-funded security.



Two senior government sources told The Telegraph that the Royal and VIP Executive Committee, the body that determines the security arrangements of high-profile figures, was likely to review the couple’s security arrangements in light of their plan to return to Britain, and that it might be easier to arrange protection when they are in the UK full-time. Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said on Thursday that the Duke and Duchess’s security was a “private matter”, despite the potential cost for taxpayers if their security were reinstated. No. 10 sources said Burnham’s comments reflected the fact that the Sussexes were private citizens, not working royals, and that their security in California was privately funded. The couple will retain their homes in Montecito, California, and Portugal, while the Duchess will continue to run her US-based lifestyle brand As Ever – which sources insist is thriving – from their new base. Despite her hiatus from acting, the Duchess has worked on a number of commercial projects with Netflix under her and her husband’s company Archewell Productions.



The Sussexes had a five-year $US100 million ($139 million) deal with the streaming service, which imploded last year amid reports published in Variety that the relationship between key executives in the company and the couple had soured. Related Article Royal family Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher During that time, the couple produced a six-part documentary on their life, a polo documentary and a lifestyle show named With Love, Meghan, that failed to make the top 1000 most-watched programmes on the streaming platform. In 2021, Andrew Morton, a royal biographer, said the late Queen had told the Duchess she was not obliged to become a full-time member of the royal family when she married Prince Harry, and could continue with her acting career should she wish. “[The Sussexes] were given a degree of latitude,” Morton told the Royally Obsessed podcast.



“They did say to Meghan: ‘If you don’t want to embrace royal duties full time, please be our guest and continue your acting career.’ Those opportunities were open to her.” The Telegraph, London Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: There’s good news for your super – but a big hole remains for retirees
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementSuperannuation Opinion There’s good news for your super – but a big hole remains for retirees Bec Wilson Money contributor August 22, 2026 — 5:09am

August 22, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Finally, the government has made its move on financial advice. And there’s plenty for us everyday people to be happy about. But there’s also a big hole in the middle that we must discuss because, ultimately, I want Australians to be able to get the help they need to make good retirement decisions. Daniel Mulino has announced the most significant changes to the financial advice regime and superannuation since the Albanese government came to power. Dominic Lorrimer Yet finding help without strings attached can be really difficult. It might be tied to the institution that already holds your money. Or it might come from an adviser with a centrally determined preferred or approved product list. Or you might find an adviser willing to give you retirement advice, but only if you also 



Because for many people, that’s when the big questions come in thick and fast: should I stay with my super fund? Should I move super funds? What type of retirement product is really right for me (versus the one my fund offers)? When should I start drawing an income stream? How does the age pension fit into my plans? And how much can I really afford to spend? Sometimes you just need someone independent to help you make some of these big decisions well. The big question is whether these reforms will finally make that kind of advice commercially attractive for advisers to offer consumers, and affordable to buy, or whether the advice industry has already moved towards a business model built around ongoing advice and investment management. The government is trying to shut the door on fear-based sales funnelling that can drive people to switch their super into dodgy schemes. Assistant Treasurer and Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino presented the government’s next stage of financial advice reforms at the National Press Club on Wednesday, with two big focuses. The first takes aim at super spruikers, lead generators and dodgy super switching – practices that have formed part of the chain of misconduct exposed by the devastating Shield and First Guardian collapses. And we should applaud these moves.



The government plans to ban unlicensed real-time communications about super. What that means is that an unlicensed super spruiker or lead generation company won’t be allowed to cold-call you, jump on a live online chat or otherwise engage you in real time to convince you to move your super. Editor's pick Opinion

Financial planning Why getting simple super advice has become an expensive nightmare Bec Wilson Money contributor These are the high-pressure interactions that happen where someone typically tells you your super is underperforming, you’re missing out or your retirement savings are at risk. Then, not long afterwards, they offer to introduce you to an adviser, or you’re told there’s a better place for your money, which ultimately leads to your super switching into high-risk, often poorly understood investments. In other words, the government is trying to shut the door on fear-based sales funnelling that can drive people to switch their super into dodgy managed investment schemes. But he’s also putting much more responsibility on the big institutions that run investment platforms. Under the reforms, ASIC will have the power to direct a super trustee, or a platform trustee, to begin compensating members if an investment option fails and there is reasonable suspicion the trustee hasn’t met their obligations.



And if the trustee is found to have breached those obligations, it will have to compensate members for 100 per cent of their capital losses. APRA will also have the power to require trustees offering higher risk investment options to have the capital backing to meet those obligations. Then, after the door to dodgy players was closed, Mulino moved onto part two – the part of the package we were all waiting for, and the one that will affect most Australians: how we actually get financial advice. There’s some good news here for almost everyone. The government is finally going to move on its long awaited Delivering Better Financial Outcomes (DBFO) reforms. Super funds will be able to reach out to members with “nudges” or prompts that encourage them to seek help. And it will become easier for funds to provide and charge for simpler types of financial advice. The cumbersome statements of advice that have helped make even quite straightforward advice expensive will also be streamlined.



And, the government will allow a new class of adviser to be offered by APRA-regulated super funds and life insurers. The goal of this is to provide a lower-cost form of advice that is within institutions that are already subject to strong regulatory oversight. There will be limits on the types of advice these advisers can provide, but they should be able to help consumers with some of the straightforward questions that, rather absurdly, super funds have struggled to answer under the current rules. Super funds will soon be able to provide more comprehensive advice to members. Dominic Lorrimer And I think that’s a superb thing. We desperately need more affordable help and support in the system. But there’s an obvious limitation. Your advice is coming from the institution that your money is already with, so while they may be able to help you make better decisions within their fund, they are not there to independently shop the market for you and tell you whether another super fund or retirement product might be better for you.



And that’s a pretty important distinction. If I’m approaching retirement, I don’t just want to know which retirement product in my existing fund might suit me next, I also want someone to tell me whether I should be in that fund at all. And if I go to an external adviser, I want to know they really are looking across the market for me, rather than being constrained by a centrally determined preferred or approved product list, designed at least in part, to make the advice business more efficient. These lists can play an important role in due diligence and risk management for advice businesses, and make providing advice more efficient. But efficiency for the advice business doesn’t always translate into a fair breadth of choice a consumer might expect when they are paying for advice. What I want is someone sitting on my side of the table, looking at my options without a predetermined destination for my money. And increasingly, I don’t know where you go to find that any more. To be fair, Mulino may have identified this problem too. Buried in Wednesday’s announcement was a commitment to reform the best interests duty to make it easier for advisers in the wider sector to provide what’s called “scaled advice” – essentially, allowing them to focus on the specific problem you’re asking about, rather than take your entire financial life into consideration.



This could be the most important part of the reforms for people approaching retirement, but the detail of the legislation will matter a lot. Because changing the rules doesn’t mean advice businesses will offer it. Another perspective Opinion

Loyalty programs Is CBA’s revamped rewards scheme worth it? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor And there’s another piece of the puzzle that hasn’t been solved: Centrelink. Because when you’re approaching retirement, you don’t make your super decisions in isolation. You need to understand how your super and the age pension will combine to deliver you a retirement income. Mulino was asked on Wednesday whether Centrelink and super funds should be able to share information so that funds could provide more comprehensive retirement guidance. He acknowledged there was a real opportunity here, saying that funds could provide better guidance if they had a basic understanding of someone’s broader financial position. And that rather proves my point – retirement advice is a lot more than super advice alone. Your super, the age pension, your other assets and your home all come together at retirement, and difficult decisions need to be made to optimise your situation. We need to make these easier to navigate.



So, while I applaud these reforms for getting the ball rolling, I think there’s a hole right in the middle. We’re making it easier to get help from the super funds that already hold our money today. And we’re making it safer to get advice by shutting down some of the very worst practices. But the real test will be whether these reforms create a market for impartial, affordable advice that consumers can buy without having to buy an investment product or sign up to an ongoing management relationship. Because at retirement, many people aren’t looking for someone to manage their money for 20 years – they just want to pay a fair and transparent fee for someone to help them make the next few decisions well. Bec Wilson is author of the bestseller How to Have an Epic Retirement and the newly released Prime Time: 27 Lessons for the New Midlife. She writes a weekly newsletter at epicretirement.net and hosts the Prime Time podcast. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Dear Prime Minister: Are you really going to let Kiwi kids best us?
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingFinancial literacy Opinion Dear Prime Minister: Are you really going to let Kiwi kids best us? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 22, 2026 — 5:01am

August 22, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dear prime minister (and come to think of it, all state and territory leaders), I write for urgent action on something that appears to have fallen off the government’s agenda: the nous of our children when they are released into the financial “wilds” at the end of their schooling. We used to have a national financial literacy strategy. This lapsed pre-COVID. We used to have the Australian Government Financial Literacy Board. This was abandoned around that same time. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon at the Parliamentary Friends of Financial Capability event at Parliament House this week. Rohan Thomson Governments here – of both flavours – used to take Australia’s collective money smarts seriously. After all, it’s make or break stuff for our lives. But let me get back to that. In 2022, responsibility for financial literacy was transferred from ASIC – which I believe was doing a bang-up job reaching many children via its lesson plans for teachers – and shifted to Treasury.



Sure, there have been some commendable efforts from the ATO. The Tax, Super + You high school competition is of special note, as is the portal’s curriculum-aligned digital learning platform and simulation games. But it is not enough. Some 70 countries now have an active financial capability strategy. And many of these have begun teaching money as a mandatory part of the school curriculum, often delivered in social sciences all the way up to year 10. Yet 8.5 million Australian adults – nearly half of us – lack basic financial literacy. We are talking Ireland, Finland, 30 states in the US, and the United Kingdom from 2028. Goodness, even New Zealand is doing it from January next year. Yet, there is no official, top-down move to fix this for Aussie kids. Don’t get me wrong, there are many excellent initiatives by many independent bodies and charities, designed to help. But there is zero guarantee that a child will receive these.





What’s more, it is becoming widely understood that financial and mental health are heavily related. Indeed, there’s now a documented bi-directional link: one can cause the other, and it can go both ways. It’s not just wealth, it’s wellbeing. And it impacts relationships and families. Yet 8.5 million Australian adults – nearly half of us – lack basic financial literacy, says new UNSW analysis of the 2016 Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia Survey (HILDA). But I was heartened by, and honoured to speak at, the first-ever Parliamentary Friends of Financial Capability event at Parliament House this week. The event was convened by Labor senator Richard Dowling and Liberal senator Jessica Collins to bring together some 200 people who believe this is a neglected issue, and never before have I been in a room where there was such agreement about the outcome needed, if not the path there. No, it’s not as simple as it is in New Zealand to introduce mandatory money lessons into schools here – we have federation, and national curriculum changes take agreement between six states and two territories. But it is now vital.



It’s not like when many older generations graduated – when the cash was gone, the cash was gone. Today, young people are the targets of technology designed to assist/relieve them of money. Indeed, until roughly 15 years ago, it was only credit cards that presented an overspending challenge, but now there is a proliferation of buy-now-pay-later and early pay services and more, amid a cost-of-living crisis. Dare I open the housing can of worms? Adding financial education to the curriculum is a no-brainer. Aresna Villanueva Our kids need help. How are they to know how to forge themselves a secure future otherwise? Because many parents feel ill-equipped to, and even anxious about, imparting these skills themselves. Please, Mr Albanese, lead the charge to get the states and territories to agree to a revised national curriculum that elevates money lessons to be mandatory. Practical, relatable, real-life ones.



Further, I ask that you urgently implement an – appropriately updated – national financial capability strategy. And I would suggest re-engaging ASIC to steer it. Of course, there needs to be funding. But surely, with the bipartisan support demonstrated at Parliament House this week, the country’s money smarts is worth it. And why would we let NZ kids get an edge on ours? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram.
