So dominant is he that it's simply not a stretch to imagine the Slovenian at the head of a rampaging UAE Team Emirates-XRG squad leading the charge to conquer the Kingdom of Spain via its mountain passes.

Of course, nothing is absolute in professional cycling.

Crashes and illness could derail Pogačar's quest to add the only one of cycling's grand tours missing from his palmares.

But rarely has there ever been a rider for whom victory seems so assured as Pogačar when he hits the front of a race.

Tadej Pogačar and Mathieu van der Poel are engaged in the most thrilling of rivalries in the Spring Classics. (Getty Images: Billy Ceusters)

As Pogačar proved during his staggeringly dominant Tour de France victory, the rest of the field was barely given a sniff.

From the moment the Slovenian star climbed away from the only man to ever claim yellow ahead of him, Jonas Vingegaard, on the slopes of the Col du Tourmalet during stage six, only the gods of misfortune ever had a hope of ripping another triumphant Paris visit from his grasp. Mere mortals cannot hope to come close enough to land a telling blow.

Pogačar crushes Tour rivals Tadej Pogačar delivers another masterclass in grand tour dominance, crushing his Tour de France rivals in one fell swoop.

So far this year, Pogačar has had 37 race days in 2026, winning 16 of them (43 per cent) as well as winning all of the three stage races he has started.

In 2025 he had 17 wins from 50 race days (34 per cent). In 2024, it was 22 wins from 58 days (38 per cent).

Victories in that time frame include three straight Tours de France, a Giro d'Italia, two world championships and a whopping eight Monument one-day races.

Such unfettered dominance is not universally acclaimed. Some of the more perniciously fickle French roadside supporters even booed Pogačar from time to time.

But some of the biggest questions have come from those who simply don't believe what they are seeing, as the curse of cycling's past looms large over the achievements of the present crop.

Alpe d'Huez record raises eyebrows

Tadej Pogačar's ascent of Alpe d'Huez was simply stunning. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

Pogačar's emphatic victory in this year's Tour de France was not a surprise.

But as a result of his latest success, and the success he has earned across races from the sport's greatest grand tours to the one-day classics of northern Europe, Pogačar cannot avoid being tainted by the shadows of the sport's nefarious past.

The spectre of doping hangs over cycling like an ancient curse, which is not far off given the century or more of scandals that have rocked the sport and its most iconic race.

As a result, winning the Tour de France is only part of the battle.

Winning over the sceptics is something else entirely, and an arguably far greater, perhaps even impossible, challenge.

Pogačar's riding at this year's race was filled with displays of verve and daring and free-spirited riding of the likes many had thought had been eliminated from the professional peloton since the advent of power meters and team radios.

Tadej Pogačar's joie de vivre is evident with every victory. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

Nothing illustrated this more than the final stage in Paris, a thrilling two-up battle with Classics rival Mathieu van der Poel that saw Pogačar pay the ultimate tribute to the jersey by relentlessly pursuing a stage win.

However, two of his five wins stand out above all others.

His sixth-stage 42-kilometre solo victory via the Col du Tourmalet was exquisite, a masterful solo attack of the like he has made his trademark since he rode himself onto the podium on stage 20 of the 2019 Vuelta a España with a similarly impressive 37km attack, which he has since repeated at the last two world championships, Liège–Bastogne–Liège and Strade Bianche.

Then, his Alpe d'Huez masterclass on stage 19 was even better, as heart-stopping a spectacle as anyone in cycling has ever seen, perhaps even the greatest single display of cycling in history.

But that ride raised even more questions, as Pogačar erased a three-and-a-half minute gap on a collection of sensational climbers ahead of him and obliterated the previous record for the 13.8km ascent of Alpe d'Huez, set by Marco Pantani during the 1995 Tour de France.

Tadej Pogačar obliterated the previous record to ride up Alpe d'Huez. (Getty Images: Luc Claessen)

Pantani's time for the ascent, 36 minutes and 40 seconds, has long been viewed with equal parts romance and scepticism.

The mid-90s were rife with drug taking in the professional peloton, with the blood-booster EPO just entering the system of the world's leading riders.

When EPO first emerged, there was no test for the drug other than to measure the percentage of blood volume made up of red blood cells.

The UCI decided that, given a percentage value of 50 per cent was at the upper limit of what a healthy adult male would have, any rider with a value above that would be sat out of a race for their own safety when tests were introduced in 1997.

That gave some riders a remit to simply top up their natural levels to be closer to that 50 per cent limit.

"If we go back to the doping era, what happened was that basically riders were getting their levels artificially raised," former Tour de France yellow jersey wearer David Millar said on the For The Love of Cycling podcast during the Tour.

"So what people were doing, they were just tweaking themselves up to those levels and so that was levelling the playing field, if you like."

David Millar (right) was a contemporary of Lance Armstrong (left). (Getty Images: Bongarts/Friedemann Vogel)

Now, with the advances in testing and the introduction of the biological passport, which tracks riders' levels over their entire career, riders that have natural advantages are allowed to thrive.

"The freaks are allowed to be freaks," Millar said.

"If we look at any elite sport … the people who are the best, they're not normal people, they're freaks.

"I think it's great now that we're getting to see these genetic freaks, with also psychological ability to be able to handle their physical gifts and do exceptional things.

"Pogačar is a poster boy of that."

Pantani, whose complicated legacy lives on in the peloton and for those who follow it, was an avid user of EPO and likely had blood the consistency of porridge when he ascended the 21 hairpins on that day.

Indeed, later in that same 1995 season, Pantani suffered a horrific crash on a descent in the Milano-Torino race. His hospital admission report noted that his hematocrit was at a hideous level of 60.1 per cent.

Pogačar's time in this year's race was 35 minutes and 27 seconds, 1 minute and 13 seconds faster than anyone has ever gone up there before.

Of course there are some areas where Pogačar has an advantage.

Marco Pantani set the fastest ascent of Alpe d'Huez in 1995, likely fueled by a cocktail of drugs. (Getty Image: Allsport/Mike Powell)

Pantani was riding a titanium-framed Carrera Titanio, a bike light years behind Pogačar's carbon fibre Colagno and its state-of-the-art wheels, which would not have weighed much more than the 6.8kg minimum limit prescribed by the UCI, aiding not just on the climb, but easing the amount of energy that riders use on the way to it.

Pogačar was also wearing lightweight, high-tech kit, had ridden fewer kilometres in the stage leading up to the climb (127km to 159km) and was the beneficiary of nutrition plans that, in the modern era, are beyond the comprehension of riders from even a handful of years ago.

In short, it's impossible to compare the two ascents properly.

But it's not stopped people from noting how jarring it is to see Pogačar's name atop a list littered with avowed dopers; Pantani appears no fewer than three times, disgraced former champion Lance Armstrong is there twice, with Jan Ullrich, Alex Zülle, Bjarne Riis and Richard Virenque also named in the list of fastest ever climbs.

"Alpe d'Huez is still something we have to process," 2012 Tour de France winner Bradley Wiggins said on The Move podcast.

"We're getting used to his insane performances … [but] we'll still be talking about that in 50 years."

'Bring me evidence', says the man who brought down Armstrong

David Walsh helped bring down Lance Armstrong. (Getty Images: David Levenson)

Journalist David Walsh will be known to many as one of the key men who brought the curtain down on Lance Armstrong's reign of chemically enhanced success at the Tour.

The result of Walsh's efforts leaves a glaring gap in the official record books between 1999 and 2005, the silence of which screams even more relentlessly into the void than the man who actually claimed the yellow jersey through those years.

Walsh's credentials for going to the ends of the earth to reveal cheaters make him a figure almost beyond reproach in the fight for clean sport.

But during this year's Tour, the veteran Irish journalist told The Cycling Podcast that he had a message to the doubters, and underlined why Pogačar was so different to the arch-villains of the past.

"For those people who may have reservations about, 'How can he be so good?' I say, just give me one reason, other than a gut feeling, other than instinct, other than a scepticism based on the past, give me one bit of what I would call serious evidence that we could go and investigate," Walsh said.

"Because nobody ever has.

"The reason why a number of people were sceptical of Lance Armstrong was there was a significant amount of evidence out there and then, when you went looking, what you found under the stone was far more damning than what brought you to the stone."

Lance Armstrong won seven straight Tour de France overall titles, but was stripped of them all. (Getty Images: TempSport/Corbis/VCG/Jean-Yves Ruszniewski)

Walsh even went as far as to say that he doesn't believe that doping is essential to win the Tour de France anymore.

"The climate has significantly changed," he said.

When Lance met Oprah Lance Armstrong had successfully doped for years. But when the evidence backed him into a corner, he took control of the narrative and confessed live on Oprah's couch, martyring himself to cycling's EPO era.

"I'm not saying that there aren't people out there still doping, still trying substances that are banned; I'm not saying that, there may well be.

"But I don't think you have to dope to win the Tour de France now. I don't believe Tadej Pogačar is doping.

"And I say that because we've had six years of him, we've seen the level he's on.

"All those dopers in the past, they didn't have even seasons because they had to give their bodies a chance to get back to normal after they had filled it up with EPO or cortisone or testosterone or human growth hormone.

"You can't be taking that stuff all the time. You had to have periods where you gave your body a chance to go back to its natural state, then start another cycle. So you had wild fluctuations in form.

"What I'm seeing now is the endless talk about nutrition, the talk about the way you train, the altitude camps, the equipment, how much lighter the bike is, the clothing, what they put into that, the amount of time they spend talking about rest, and the off-the-bike work they're doing.

"We're at a point now, [where] we have a generation of cyclists now who thinks: 'There's loads of ways I can improve, whether it's nutrition or training or resting, whatever; there are lots of ways I can improve.'

"In the old days, there was only one way you improved: you doped."

Doping questions will never go away

Cycling may well be destined to forever be tainted by the stain of its past. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

As Pogačar lines up with the rest of the professional peloton in Monaco this weekend for the start of the Vuelta, it's clear that the stain of cycling's past will never wash away.

Even when it was revealed that Pogačar and Vingegaard had been woken up in the early hours of the morning for a surprise doping test during the Tour de France, it was accepted as something that simply had to happen to maintain any semblance of respectability and credibility.

If, as it is expected, Pogačar wins in Spain, then heads to Canada and wins the world championships for a third-straight time, what does that say about the sport that one man can be so dominant?

The Vuelta is likely to be contested at a rip-roaring pace, just as the Tour de France was before it, completed at an average speed of 43.227km/h for its 3,482km, the fastest average speed in history.

In 1995, when Miguel Induráin won, the average speed for the entire 3,635km of racing was 39.193km/h.

The peloton didn't achieve an average of over 40km/h until 1999, the first year of the since-annulled Armstrong era and the world knows all too well what that speed increase was fuelled by.

As performances continue to improve, and Pogačar continues to produce some of the most spellbinding riding you'll ever see across mountains and cobbles and days and weeks, the questions will always exist.

That is the price the sport must pay for the sins of the past.

When is the Vuelta a España?

The only previous time Tadej Pogačar has raced the Vuelta, he rode into third place overall with a solo attack on the penultimate stage as a 20-year-old. (Getty Images: Justin Setterfield)

The Vuelta gets underway on August 22 in Monaco and runs through to September 13 where it will finish in Granada.

Riders will race 21 stages and will cover a total distance of 3,275km.

How can I watch the Vuelta a España in Australia?

SBS will have live coverage of the race on SBS, SBS Viceland and SBS On Demand.

World.title: Why Wallaroos are connected by 'family' bond as they play 100th Test
World.content:
When you chat about the Wallaroos with Libby Andrew, one word frequently comes up in conversation.

Family.

It's the description Andrew uses to explain the close-knit relationship between players who have represented the national women's rugby union team, both past and present.

She knows, as well as anyone, how deep the connection runs, having played in the Wallaroos' first Test in 1994.

When Andrew was asked to present Wallaroos players with their jerseys last year, the strength of the bond was clear to see.

"I had never met any of them face to face," Andrew told ABC Sport this week.

"But when I walked into that room, there was a connection there.

"I guess it's probably a bit like being a grandparent. It feels like family."

Libby Andrew (third from left in front row) was asked to present the Wallaroos with their jerseys in 2025. (Supplied)

The 2026 Wallaroos squad share Andrew's sentiment.

"There is just something that still ties you together, whether you're a Wallaroo of today's era or the past," Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said.

"The experiences that you have on the field and off the field — they can only be felt by those who are Wallaroos."

Palu Sekona is preparing to lead the Wallaroos in Saturday afternoon's O'Reilly Cup Test against New Zealand in Auckland.

It will be the Wallaroos' 100th Test after a 32-year journey to reach the milestone.

Siokapesi Palu Sekona says she is honoured to captain the Wallaroos in their 100th Test. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

When Palu Sekona and her teammates take the field against the Black Ferns, they'll be playing for more than themselves.

"There is definitely a responsibility to not only do the jersey justice, but to honour and show respect to the trailblazers of the game," said Palu Sekona, who will start at blindside flanker.

"I want to make sure I lead this team well and it will be a reflection of not only the 23 players who wear that jersey [against New Zealand], but more so for all the Wallaroos who are embedded in those green and gold jerseys."

Wallaroos' early days

Despite the fact history was made at North Sydney Oval on September 2, 1994, the Wallaroos' first Test was an understated occasion.

The squad to play New Zealand was picked following a national invitational club tournament held in Newcastle, as there was no official interstate competition — like Super Rugby Women's — in those days.

Andrew, who started in rugby league before switching codes, was one of several ACT players chosen.

The Test kicked off at 5pm as the first match of a double-header, with a Shute Shield semifinal between Randwick and Warringah considered the main attraction.

Libby Andrew played 12 Tests for the Wallaroos. (Supplied)

"We got stuck in peak-hour traffic on a Friday in Sydney and we were pushing shit uphill from the afternoon we left the hotel," said Andrew, who was a reserve flanker for the Test.

"At the time, I was so focused on the game that I had no idea we were creating history. It never occurred to me.

"I wasn't thinking about how other people were going to receive it or what it was going to feel like.

"We arrived late. There was no jersey presentation. It was like, 'We're late, the traffic was heavy, here's your jersey and chuck it on.'"

New Zealand won the Test 37-0, but the moment deserved to be remembered as a victory for Australian women's rugby.

The Australian Rugby Football Union (ARFU) — now known as Rugby Australia (RA) — had expressed lukewarm interest in establishing a national women's team.

ARFU staff member Joan Forno, who had been appointed Australian Women's Rugby Union president in 1993, took on the responsibility.

"She kept asking why aren't the girls playing and they kept ignoring her," Andrew said.

"We had missed the first two World Cups and I think because of the success of the Wallabies at the time, people were asking where the girls' team was.

"The ARFU kind of said, 'We're going to have to do this at some point'.

"They asked Joan if she would get it off the ground."

How Australia won historic Olympic gold It may be 10 years since Australia won gold in women's rugby sevens at the Rio Olympics, but the impact of the victory will be felt for generations to come.

In Forno, Australian women's rugby had found one of its greatest advocates.

The players were juggling match and training commitments with full-time work or study, while some also had parenting duties.

Others quit their jobs so they could play for the national team.

Forno fought for funding, resourcing and — above all — greater recognition of the women's game.

"Joan Forno is like your mother," said Andrew, who worked as a police officer during her playing career.

"You don't say no to Joan Forno. Everyone was petrified of Joan, but Joan got shit done.

"I'm really hoping when the Women's Rugby World Cup comes to Australia in 2029, there will be credit given to Joan Forno."

The Wallaroos collected the Plate in their first Women's Rugby World Cup appearance. (Getty Images: Tom Honan)

Forno managed the Wallaroos when they made their Women's Rugby World Cup debut at the 1998 tournament, which was held in Amsterdam.

Under her management and the coaching of another devoted supporter of women's rugby, Bob Hitchcock, the Wallaroos reached the quarterfinals where they lost to England 30-13.

But the Wallaroos later defeated Scotland 25-15 to claim the Plate title.

"Joan and Bobby Hitchcock were like a pigeon pair," said Andrew, who played in the 1998 and 2002 Women's Rugby World Cups.

"Without Joan and Bob, there's no way we would be where we were."

'For the love of the game'

To mark the 30th anniversary of the Wallaroos' first Test, Andrew was inspired to self-publish a book in which she reflected on the team's history and the challenges they faced.

Wallaroos name new head coach As the Wallaroos edge closer to becoming a full-time program, a key appointment has been made in the build-up to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

The book was titled Wallaroo 19 (Andrew is officially recognised as the 19th Wallaroos representative).

The fact the Wallabies were fully professional for much of Andrew's Test career, while Wallaroos players held down jobs, isn't lost on the 54-year-old.

"The women's rugby era I came from, we did things for our mates and for the love of the game," said Andrew, who played 12 Tests between 1994-2002.

"If it wasn't us, it may not have happened until 10 years later.

"The experience of a female athlete in this country was not the same experience as a man in the same sport."

Siokapesi Palu Sekona regards the original Wallaroos as trailblazers. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Palu Sekona is in awe of the legacy forged by Andrew and her teammates.

"They've been the trailblazers," Palu Sekona said.

"They had to make those sacrifices at the beginning."

Positive steps

As Australia prepares to host the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup, RA is increasing its support of the Wallaroos.

In a long overdue move, the Wallaroos' squad will soon go full-time and be aligned with the women's sevens program.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Overseeing this process will be successful Australian sevens coach Tim Walsh, who began work as RA's director of women's high-performance last month.

Walsh's knowledge of the rugby landscape is outstanding and he's ideally suited for this role, having been in charge of the women's sevens program when it went full-time in 2014.

He'll work closely with incoming Wallaroos head coach, Sione Fukofuka, who begins his tenure next year.

Walsh realises the Wallaroos are a "sleeping giant" in international rugby as their potential hasn't been properly harnessed.

Naysayers will point out the Wallaroos have lost more than 60 per cent of their Tests, remain winless against New Zealand after 30 attempts and finished no higher than third in their eight appearances at the Women's Rugby World Cup.

But these results create a false impression about Australia's talent pool and only highlight the hurdles women's rugby has faced, such as underfunding.

"The term sleeping giant is a really good analogy," Walsh said.

"We've seen glimpses of it (Wallaroos' potential). We've got the athletes, but we've got to provide the infrastructure for them to be able to excel.

"The runway to a home World Cup is long enough to wake up that giant."

Walsh added: "The physicality, the skill acquisition and the amount of times you get to play against and with each other is probably what's lacking.

"What we're looking to do is to maximise talent. There are some great players out there."

The Wallaroos' on-field performances will improve in a full-time environment. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

For Palu Sekona, who balances playing commitments alongside her job at Canberra's Erindale College, the Wallaroos just need "the opportunity to hone their rugby craft".

"Once we get our physicality right, our strength and conditioning right, imagine where our game can take us," said Palu Sekona, who plays her 28th Test on Saturday.

Andrew is elated the Wallaroos will get the support they lacked during her career.

"If those girls get full-time contracts, I can only say Hallelujah," she said.

"We do have the talent. We just need the coaching and we need the same opportunities the other countries have got."

Living in Canberra, Andrew will be with the Wallaroos in spirit once kick-off rolls around in Auckland at 1:05pm AEST.

When asked how proud she'll be watching the Wallaroos play their 100th Test, Andrew's sense of family came to the fore again.

"[I'll be] like a mother watching her child ride a bike for the first time," she said.

World.title: Once-famed 'Bloods culture' dead as scandal highlights respect issue
World.content:
The disturbing and potentially criminal events at the Pullman Hotel last Monday morning have triggered the darkest chapter in Sydney Swans' history and spotlighted a sordid AFL underbelly.

The most serious allegation is that one of the players sexually assaulted a woman by touching her without consent.

None have been charged, and while the police investigation is ongoing, these events are creating a greater conversation around the AFL's handling of allegations of violence against women.

The woman who alleges she has been sexually assaulted has said she will fight.

"I am going to stand up for what is right," she told the Herald Sun on Thursday.

Lawyer speaks Three women at the centre of the Sydney Swans sexual assault scandal are suffering "severe trauma" but are receiving support, their lawyer says.

This latest incident has highlighted the lack of a clear "no-fault stand-down" policy in the AFL — one that has successfully been in place in the NRL.

Looking back at the last 16 years, there have been a number of AFL footballers charged with crimes such as sexual assault, rape and indecent assault, and the league has imposed varying penalties. Not one player has been convicted.

An AFL player had his contract ripped up in 2010 (his rape charges were later dropped).

In 2020, Collingwood superstar Jordan De Goey was charged with indecent assault of a woman. He played on.

In 2021, Victoria Police had to pay legal costs to De Goey after it dropped a historical indecent assault charge against him.

When Geelong star Tanner Bruhn was charged with rape and intentional sexual touching, the AFL stood him down from playing for the entire 2025 season.

Bruhn also sought a suppression order so his name was never public and he sat out Geelong's season with a reported "finger" injury. Those charges against Bruhn were dropped last November, when a key witness admitted to lying.

Previously, the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) has pushed back against a no-fault stand-down policy, which the NRL has used to great effect; it's a rule that means players facing serious charges involving women are automatically barred from playing footy.

After the charges were dropped, a telling moment came in November last year, when the AFLPA issued a firm statement opposing the young footballer Bruhn being stood down from playing for the entire season.

"Tanner was entitled to the presumption of innocence from the outset and throughout. It was clear to us that standing Tanner down would be premature and disproportionate," the AFLPA said in a statement in November last year.

The statement said the AFLPA would like to "resolve" a code of conduct with the AFL "including proper processes and a sanctioning framework".

"We remain committed to this work in the best interests of the players and Australian football," the AFLPA said.

Earlier this year, on the eve of Bruhn's first game in 17 months, Geelong coach Chris Scott was highly supportive of his player.

"It's just fantastic for him to get out there and be able to concentrate on footy after what is one of the most egregious injustices I can think of in the game," Scott said.

Misogynistic AFL culture needs reckoning Swans chairperson Andrew Pridham claims his players have "complete respect for women", but the week's events call for a reckoning with AFL culture.

When contacted this week, an AFLPA spokesperson said the association had previously opposed a blanket no-fault stand-down policy, but was open to discussing it.

The NRL implemented its no-fault stand-down policy seven years ago and believes it has shifted culture.

That policy automatically removes players from playing if they are charged with a serious criminal offence carrying a maximum prison sentence of 11 years or more.

It was introduced in March 2019 and applies on full pay without prejudging the footballer's guilt.

Just months after the NRL put it in place, Dragons star Jack De Belin, then up on a sexual assault charge, opposed the stand-down policy in the Federal Court and lost.

Federal Court Justice Melissa Perry dismissed de Belin's legal challenge against the Australian Rugby League Commission and the NRL, ruling it a lawful measure to protect the game's reputation.

The NRL chief executive also has the discretionary power to stand down players whose charges involve women or children, regardless of the jail term.

The NRL is proud of this policy, which was driven by key commissioners, including former Queensland premier Peter Beattie, professor Megan Davis and now league chair Peter V'landys.

Insiders say it has been monumental in helping improve culture in the game.

While in AFL there has been the rise of the AFLW competition and more women are commentating the game, and in influential positions in footy clubs than ever before, this week, one prominent woman in the industry called out a festering "horrific misogyny".

Commentator and former player Kate McCarthy said the AFL needed to look deeply at its culture and inclusion of women.

Kate McCarthy has spoken out in reaction to Monday's events. (Getty Images: Hancock)

She told the Herald Sun earlier in the week that language used by Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich in initially addressing the matter on Monday concerned her.

Pavlich spoke about the Swans players finding "themselves in this situation".

"Is there really any surprise that women within the industry experience such horrific misogyny when the role models or people in positions of power like CEOs of clubs use language saying that the 'players found themselves in this situation,'" McCarthy said.

It's also only two weeks ago AFL Hall of Famer and former Geelong footballer Sam Newman drew outrage for his comments on former AFL player manager Ralph Carr being found guilty of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault.

"I'm just wondering what sort of evidence they had about him raping her," Newman said on his podcast. "Other than the fact she might have buyer's remorse."

Newman, at last check, maintains his AFL Hall of Fame status. This is despite the AFL stating it takes in "integrity" and "character" when it comes to holding the status.

In June this year, St Kilda great Nicky Winmar was swiftly removed from the AFL Hall of Fame after he was found guilty of three assault charges against a woman.

The sexual assault allegation against the Swans has moved those holding Australia's highest offices to make statements.

The prime minister said the "AFL certainly has to do better" and raised the NRL's leading stand-down policy on 7.30 on Thursday night.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn, a former Swans board member for six seasons, said her thoughts were with the alleged victim and that she was "shocked and troubled" by the allegations involving the team.

Sam Mostyn spent six seasons on the Swans' board. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"At times like this, we are reminded to never take for granted the need for constant vigilance for respectful treatment of women everywhere; across clubs, the AFL, sport, and the community generally," she told ABC.

"Sadly, the lack of respect for women across the country remains an issue for us all to be concerned about, particularly in sport."

The governor-general added she believed there should be more women in positions of power and influence not only in the AFL but all sporting codes.

Whether the AFL acts on this week's events, making firm policy and broader change, remains to be seen.

In the meantime, this scandal has raised a disturbing question: has the AFL's inaction in installing a strict policy that ensures that all players are stood down automatically when they are charged with a crime against a woman created an environment where players are not wholly focused on the issue of ensuring respect for women?

Putting the most grave and serious allegation of sexual assault to the side, the reports that players felt comfortable hiring adult entertainers, allegedly doing drugs off the women's bodies and were drinking well into the early hours of Monday two weeks out from finals, have also spotlighted the fact the once-famed "Bloods culture" has run dead.

Former Swans captain Kieran Jack, who led the team to a premiership in 2012, said he felt "devastated" and "very troubled" by players' actions and that Bloods culture "feels broken".

Bloods culture had previously been lauded. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He notably said a "lack of respect for women" cannot be tolerated.

"'Bloods culture' is often spoken about," Jack wrote on Instagram. "This was built and maintained through a core pillar of respect. Respect for each other, respect for the club, your family, the opponent, supporters and importantly, community. Right now this feels broken. A lack of respect for women cannot be tolerated."

The Bloods culture, which was created by club coach Paul Roos and players like workhorse midfielder Brett Kirk, was founded on humility, discipline, selflessness and hard work.

More than 20 years ago, the Swans established this true team-first culture. If one player in the group broke the team rules, all would pay.

There were secret punishment sessions conducted before sunrise, and they often involved players turning up in the cold to do additional strenuous physical training like push-ups on the asphalt with their bare knuckles. These sessions were player-led and enforced.

There were no individual sponsorships with toothpaste companies. No rock-star midfielders. Players were encouraged "not to go down media street" and do unnecessary publicity.

Heading into the 2005 grand final, the Swans midfield was likened to the basic car brand "Ford Cortinas" coming up against the West Coast Eagles midfield made up of "Lamborghinis". The Swans beat the Eagles by a point and broke a 72-year premiership drought.

As Kirk said after that premiership, it was a group of men who could unequivocally trust one another. "It's hard to put a measure on it, but what you do know is that you have 100 per cent commitment and trust that the guys you're playing with that sacrifice and do anything for you, that they'll never let you down," Kirk said.

But as sources familiar with that period of time remarked this week, the Bloods culture had been betrayed, and some noted their famed unofficial "no dickheads policy" had truly been abandoned.

"We have to stop on occasions believing our own bullshit," one remarked.

John Longmire, who coached the team to the 2012 flag and was at the helm of the club until 2024, said he was saddened by the events and it would take time for the club to climb its way out of the darkness.

John Longmire (file photo) says the Swans will have to rebuild trust. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

"The culture of the footy club has taken a big hit, and it will take time for everyone to rebuild the trust in the football club," he told Fox Footy this week.

Swans chair Andrew Pridham said he was "very proud" of the club culture. However, some believe it has been brutally exposed as having serious cultural issues when it comes to women.

But it's an issue that extends beyond the Swans, one that should trigger deep evaluation and a review. It's absolutely a review that should extend past the Swans' $70 million Moore Park clubrooms into the AFL in general.

As former AFLW player McCarthy expertly put it: "The AFL talks a lot about wanting women and girls to feel that football belongs to them.

"That can't only mean having an AFLW competition or getting more women through the gates.

"It also means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated and how the industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise."

World.title: McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies
World.content:
Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

The Lions went into the final round with a 2.2 per cent advantage over the Hawks.

A dominant display against the Magpies at the MCG saw the Lions emerge with a 63-point victory, 25.9 (159) to 15.6 (96) that gives them a 4.4 per cent lead over their rivals.

However Hawthorn has the advantage of playing West Coast in Perth on Sunday, needing a winning margin of somewhere in the region of 100 points to overtake the Lions.

Logan Morris kicked eight goals, and Irishman Conor McKenna kicked four, including a soccered dink of a goal in the first half, and a blind snap on the turn from 45 in the third quarter.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan told Fox Footy his side would "absolutely have taken it" if offered top-four at the start of the year.

Logan Morris is leading the way in attack for the Brisbane Lions against Collingwood at the MCG. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

Collingwood coach Craig McRae said the game was a hard watch at times as a coach given the lack of defence - the Pies kicked seven goals in a wide-open final term and the Lions booted nine.

But McRae was clear on what he and his team had seen from the Lions.

"Clearly we played the best team in the competition," he told reporters.

"They've got gears ... like we haven't seen a team do (this year), they can put you away so quickly."

Magpies great Scott Pendlebury is under an injury cloud after ending his game with a knee bursa issue.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Brisbane boys go back to back with stunning come-from-behind wins
World.content:
Brisbane has mounted a stunning second-half fightback to deny Josh Papali'i a win in his final game at Canberra Stadium before the Dolphins shook off another slow start to take down the Eels.

The loss ended the Raiders' faint finals hopes after they looked on track for a celebratory victory while leading 30-16 with 18 minutes left in the retiring Papali'i's hometown farewell.

But 18 straight points, capped saw the Broncos to a 34-30 win in scenes reminiscent of their comeback win at the same ground in last year's finals series, albeit in much lower stakes and far more conventional fashion.

At Lang Park, the Dolphins consolidated their place in the league's top four with a 34-16 win over the Eels after they too trailed 10-0 after just 20 minutes.

The Dolphins have made a habit of relying on their sparkling attack to fire them back from slow starts, and it has now carried them to five straight wins and four points clear of Cronulla in fourth spot.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Australia names team for second Test against Bangladesh
World.content:
Australia have resisted the temptation to play four specialist fast bowlers against Bangladesh in the second Test in Mackay, as captain Pat Cummins confirmed Matt Renshaw would open the batting.

The recalled Renshaw is a straight swap for Jake Weatherald, who was dropped after six underwhelming Test matches.

The pitch at Great Barrier Reef Arena is expected to assist the pacemen, but off spinner Nathan Lyon, after taking 1-102 in the first innings of the nine-wicket loss by Australia in Darwin, will play his 143rd Test.

Australia vs Bangladesh second Test preview Winter cricket continues in the Top End, with Australia looking for a big response in the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay.

Outstanding paceman Scott Boland did not play in Darwin and will now have to wait until the tour of South Africa in October for his next Test, after starring in last summer's Ashes.

Pitch curator Peter Kazakoff said the Mackay wicket would suit fast bowlers on both sides.

"That is what we are aiming for, a lot of pace," he said.

"We want the ball to come through really nicely. We have got the same sort of clay as the Gabba, so we are expecting similar sort of characteristics to that."

Australia confirmed their side, with Lyon in it, an hour after captain Cummins held a press conference where he said he was considering an all-out pace attack.

Kazakoff said there would be a role for Lyon and the Bangladesh spinners.

"I think the spinners will come into the game, going off previous first-class games here," he said.

"Spinners have had a big say later in the match. Obviously those first-class games were a bit later in the year when it was a bit warmer.

"It is a lot cooler this time of year. The moisture will come out of the wicket less and slower."

There has been a lot of talk about "soul-searching" in the Australian camp after the Darwin loss, but Cummins said he was confident of a response.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"In home Test matches we pride ourselves on winning as many as we can," he said.

"It's funny. I think if we played really well and we lost you'd feel like we needed to do some soul-searching.

"I certainly felt like we didn't play anywhere near our best and they played really well. When we play well, fortunately we have got a decent body of work to look back on."

Weatherald's axing was simple to explain for Cummins, who said he was "awesome around the group" but did not deliver.

"Over the course of six Test matches he didn't quite score the runs he or we would have liked," Cummins said.

Renshaw, 30, will play his first Test in three years after averaging 49.9 in Sheffield Shield cricket last summer, including scoring three centuries.

"[Renshaw] has been really impressive and had some great off-season tours of Pakistan and Bangladesh recently with white-ball (formats). He looks in good nick," Cummins said.

"He had a really good Shield season last season.

"Some of the kind of chat about [Renshaw] in the past is that he can look different from day to day.

"When you get to the back half of your career as a batter you want to really know what you look like at your best, and I think he does that.

"I hope he brings his best version every day, is nice and sharp and puts the pressure on the bowlers."

Australia XI for second Test: Matthew Renshaw, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wk), Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (c), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood

AAP

World.title: Swans AFLW captain and coach say club is 'united' amid scandal
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy has said her players have had "open conversations" in the wake of the scandal that has engulfed her club and led to five men's players being suspended for the rest of the season.

McEvoy, along with AFLW coach Colin O'Riordan, spoke to the media on Friday afternoon, saying the women's program supports the sanctions imposed on Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. The press conference has ended AFLW players would like to have say in whether five suspended men's players return Lucy McEvoy is asked if the AFLW players have discussed whether they want the five suspended players to return to the club. She tells the media that conversation has not happened but, when the time comes, the AFLW players would like to be part of the discussion. 'Moment for all women to stand together', McEvoy Here is more from Lucy McEvoy, speaking about the wider issue at the heart of this week's scandal. "There's no doubt, I think, a lot of women in the community are all feeling the same. "It's obviously an issue within the community that needs to be addressed, and I think this week it has been. "I applaud the club in the way they have handled it, and respected us as a women's program. "I think it's an important moment for all women to stand together and understand that all women deserve respect." Show more

Those five players will miss the remainder of the AFL season following club-imposed suspensions for breaking team standards in Melbourne earlier this week.

Victoria Police are investigating a sexual assault allegation, where it is alleged one player touched a woman without her consent. No charges have been laid, and no-one has been formally interviewed.

Speaking on Friday, McEvoy said the AFLW program supported the club-imposed suspensions to the five men's players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.

"On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down," McEvoy said.

"To the players, we are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people were.

"We know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club."

McEvoy said it had been a big week for the women's program, who will face Essendon at the Sydney Cricket Ground this weekend.

The Swans were hoping to celebrate this week's double-header with the men's round 24 clash with North Melbourne following the AFLW match on Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of this week's scandal, McEvoy said members of the women's program were processing their emotions and the situation.

"We've had some really open conversations as a group this week, and with the club more broadly," she said.

"We've felt the support both internally and externally as well.

"The girls are working through their emotions as they see fit for themselves."

When asked how this week has affected the reputation of the Sydney Swans, McEvoy said the club, both men's and women's teams, must work to regain the public's trust.

"There's no doubt the club has taken a reputational hit," she said.

"We will do whatever we can as a club, both programs, to make sure we build back the trust and respect of our members and fans, and the community more broadly."

O'Riordan, who played 34 AFL matches for the Swans between 2015 and 2022 before becoming the club's AFLW coach this season, said he was disappointed that he had to address this scandal.

"The actions of a small number of people have impacted a lot of people, especially the women in our football club and wider community," he said.

"As a man who was brought up with strong morals and a strong sense of what is right and wrong, [it's] disappointing to be standing here today and be talking about something like this.

"Growing up, I was always taught you treat everyone with respect, and that respect is a fundamental pillar of how you live your life.

"That is especially important in how you treat women."

O'Riordan said the club had remained "incredibly united" in the wake of the scandal.

"This is a united club. It always has been and always will be," he said.

Tech.title: Apple is laying off staffers working on the Vision Pro and Siri
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is laying off staff on the Siri and the Vision Pro teams, according to Bloomberg. The cuts include “largely shutting down” a Vision Pro gaming team and “reducing the size” of the team that makes Vision Pro immersive content, the publication says. More than 200 jobs were cut.

Apple said in a statement to Bloomberg it was making the changes to “to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users,” though it will be making new roles. The company didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge.

The Vision Pro launched in early 2024 as Apple’s big bet on “spatial computing,” but the $3,499 headset doesn’t appear to have been a big hit. While Bloomberg reported in May that Apple is working on “a slimmer and lighter headset” to succeed the current Vision Pro (which was updated last year with an M5 chip), a report a few weeks after said that Apple was suspending work with Samsung Display on a display for an entry-level XR machine.

However, following the success of Meta’s smart glasses, Apple is apparently planning to make its own smart glasses, with Bloomberg reporting recently that Apple plans to announce them at WWDC (typically a June event) in 2027 and launch them by the end of that year.

The company finally launched its revamped, AI-powered Siri at this year’s WWDC. The new Siri is set to be available to the public in beta later this year.

Tech.title: $100 Best Buy gift cards will be $60 at stores Saturday
Tech.content:
The best gift card deal we’ve spotted this year is happening Saturday, August 22nd, at Best Buy stores for one day only. In celebration of the retailer’s 60th anniversary, you can purchase a $100 Best Buy gift card for $60. The deal is only good for as long as supplies last at your local store, so you might want to plan on getting there no later than opening time to boost your chance of getting one.

There are some limitations on how you can use the gift card. You can’t use them to buy other gift cards, like iTunes or Google Play credit, and they also can’t be used to buy prepaid or open-loop debit cards. However, they can be used in combination with other discounts or promotions on products from Best Buy, and any returns or cancellations you make will credit back to the gift card.

We’ve found a number of deals during Best Buy’s 60th anniversary sale that you can apply that gift card to. The iPad Air M4 dropped to $649, the lowest we’ve seen since the prices went up this summer, and the AirPods Max 2 are only $429, $120 lower than their usual price. There are a variety of discounts on Windows and macOS laptops too, like this HP OmniBook X Flip 2-in-1 for $749.99, a $450 discount from the typical price.

Tech.title: Walmart is finally adding Apple Pay and Google Pay
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Walmart will soon allow you to pay for your items with Google Pay or Apple Pay. In an announcement on Friday, Walmart says it’s going to bring tap-to-pay capabilities to “select” Walmart and Sam’s Club locations starting August 24th, before rolling out support to all US stores by the end of 2026 and gas stations by mid-2027.

This launch has been a long time coming, as Walmart was one of the last major retailers not to support Apple Pay or Google Pay. The retail giant even backed the launch of the short-lived CurrentC mobile payment service before rolling out Walmart Pay in 2016, which lets you quickly check out with a QR code at its stores. A Walmart spokesperson doubled down on its decision not to support NFC-based payments in a statement to MacRumors last year, saying the company offers “convenient solutions” like Walmart Pay instead. But now, the company seems to have changed its tune.

“We want customers and members to have choice in how they pay, so they can check out in the way that works best for them,” Walmart’s announcement says. “Tap to Pay is a great addition to the other payment options already offered like cash, credit card or Walmart Pay.”

Tech.title: Microsoft and Discord subpoenaed over GTA VI gameplay leaks
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series

Following several apparent video leaks of Grand Theft Auto VI, Take-Two Interactive has subpoenaed Microsoft and Discord over content that “infringes copyrights” held for the game, Kotaku reports. In the subpoenas, filed on Thursday, Take-Two says copyrighted material includes “audiovisual content, artwork, images, dialogue, or other creative elements” and it is looking to identify “alleged infringers at issue.” The subpoenas give Microsoft and Discord until September 4th to produce the requested information.

The leaked clips have been watermarked by a person or group going by “CyberLeek,” and they have shown what appears to be GTA VI protagonist Jason Duval (one of two protagonists) doing various activities, including driving, flying an airplane, using a taser, and attacking somebody with a wrench. In one clip, the player spells “LEEK” by shooting holes in a wall.

Discord and Microsoft didn’t immediately reply to requests for comment. On X, Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet says that “We are working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support efforts to protect creative works and intellectual property.”

The leaks have popped up ahead of Rockstar’s big extended preview of the game that is set to debut on Netflix on August 27th. The full game is scheduled to launch on November 19th.

Update, August 21st: Added statement from Xbox’s CTO.

Tech.title: Pixel 11 gets in on the digicam trend
Tech.content:
I recently looked back at a photo I’d taken on a smartphone in 2014, and I was struck by just how good it looked. The details were soft, the shadows were dark. It was the kind of photo I felt like I hadn’t seen out of a phone in years. That might be changing, though. The Pixel 11 includes a suite of new photography features called Camera Looks that allow those who really care about those things (hi, it’s all of us) to dial in their preferences and get rid of that modern over-processed look.

On today’s episode of The Vergecast, David Imel joins us to discuss his time reviewing the Pixel 11 Pro and how he’s thinking about its new approach to computational photography. After that, we’ve got a super-sized edition of Brendan Carr is a Dummy, everyone’s favorite podcast with a podcast. It was a big week for bad telecom policy, and we’re giving it the time it deserves. Tech.title: Why does it seem like food recalls are out of control this year?
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Just weeks after Taylor Farms issued a recall of its iceberg lettuce amid a massive cyclospora outbreak, the Food and Drug Administration recalled more than one million eggs that may be contaminated with salmonella. The eggs, which come from Midwest Poultry Services, were distributed to Kroger and smaller grocery stores across the South and Southwest US. Then, Taylor Farms pulled more than a dozen of its products containing jalapeños — including guacamole, salsa, taco dip, and more — from store shelves after its supplier, Coast Citrus Distributors, recalled fresh peppers due to salmonella contamination.

The list of major recalls that occurred over the past few months doesn’t end there, as frozen blueberries and mixed berries sold at Publix stores in multiple states were recalled over concerns about E. coli contamination earlier this month. Some of Outshine’s fruit bars were also removed for potential glass contamination, while even dog food and eye drops have been affected by recent recalls. Altogether, the recent recalls have sickened thousands of people (and some dogs) across the US.

Darin Detwiler, professor emeritus at Northeastern and adjunct professor at Michigan State University College of Law, tells The Verge that available data from the FDA suggests that “recall activity has indeed been elevated,” but notes that it’s “too early to know” whether this year’s recalls will outpace the ones issued in 2025.

“This is where recall fatigue can become trust fatigue.”

As of July 31st, we’ve had 122 food and beverage recalls so far this year, compared to 135 during the same period in 2025 and 146 in 2024, according to the Poynter Institute. “We just transitioned through the summer, which for various reasons tends to see more foodborne outbreaks than other months,” Edward Dudley, a professor of food science at Pennsylvania State University, tells The Verge. “There has been an increased effort to highlight these events by media outlets, which is great for public awareness, but doesn’t necessarily reflect a concerning uptick in risk.”

While the current number of recalls may not be significantly higher than previous years, a report from the US Public Interest Research Group notes that we have still seen “a huge increase” in outbreaks of foodborne illnesses. “What we can say is that recall activity in 2026 appears elevated, and some individual recalls are affecting extraordinarily large quantities of food,” Detwiler says. “That distinction matters. A handful of very large recalls can expose far more consumers than dozens of smaller events.” The lettuce-linked cyclospora outbreak contributed to more than 9,000 illnesses in the US, which may make it the third-largest recorded outbreak of foodborne illnesses, according to the PIRG.

Some of these large and small events have been getting a lot of attention. News outlets and television stations have picked up on the recalls published by the FDA and US Department of Agriculture. Online personalities often joined the chorus with their viral recall warning posts racking up thousands of likes and views, bolstered by social media algorithms.

“When recall notices become part of the background noise of everyday life, people may stop paying attention,” Detwiler adds. “Worse, they may begin accepting recalls and outbreaks as simply an unavoidable cost of operating a complex food system… This is where recall fatigue can become trust fatigue.”

The Trump administration’s federal funding cuts may also make it more challenging for agencies to oversee food safety. The FDA’s budget decreased by $271 million compared to last year. It also cut over 4,300 employees in 2025 and 2026, while the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention slashed over 2,800 jobs, as reported by FoodNavigator. In February, the Government Accountability Office said the FDA is currently dealing with staffing shortages as the number of required safety inspections increases.

It also doesn’t help that the CDC pulled back on efforts to track certain foodborne diseases last year, with pathogens like cyclospora, listeria, and shigella no longer included in its surveillance program. The FDA also delayed the deadline to comply with the Traceability Rule, a law that introduces new record-keeping requirements for businesses that manufacture, process, pack, or hold certain kinds of food, including fresh leafy greens, peppers, eggs, tomatoes, and more. The goal of the law is to make it easier to track and remove contaminated food. It was supposed to go into effect in January 2026, but the FDA pushed back its enforcement to 2028.

With fewer federal staff members and looser regulations, efforts to better detect, track, and avoid recalls become more difficult. “The solution is not to communicate less about recalls,” Detwiler adds. “It is to prevent more of them, communicate clearly when they occur, explain what went wrong, strengthen the institutions responsible for detecting hazards, and demonstrate that lessons from previous failures are actually being implemented.”

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 10A is a great deal at 15 percent off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This week, all of Google’s Pixel 11 phones launched, including the $899 Pixel 11, the $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro (with the same processor and starting 12GB RAM as the standard model, but with better cameras), and the $1,899 Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re good phones, but if you don’t mind missing out on their new, exclusive camera and AI features, you can get a great Google-made phone that’s hundreds less.

Google’s Pixel 10A has been sitting at an attractive $424 (originally $499) at Amazon, Best Buy, and at the Google Store since early August, and we’re just highlighting it again here today in case you’re shopping for a phone.

An IP68 rating, 90Hz refresh rate screen, wireless charging, and great design aren’t something you have to pay close to $1,000 to get. Similar to Apple’s iPhone 17E (but with slightly older parts by direct comparison), the Pixel 10A offers many of the same hardware and software features as previous Pixels. Its camera specs and Tensor G4 processor — debuted within the Pixel 9 series — are the biggest differences between the 10A and pricier versions. Our criticism of the 10A focused on how little Google changed compared to the 9A, yet it’s still a good phone if you haven’t upgraded in a while. Read our review.
